newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Further EU Beef, BSE battles seen first half 1997.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Further EU Beef, BSE battles seen first half 1997.

text.p: The European Union faces more rows over Britain's beef crisis in the first half of 1997 as member states debate long-term reforms to deal with "mad cow" disease and London works to ease a worldwide ban on British cattle.
"Beef reforms and BSE are likely to dominate the presidency agenda," said a Dutch official, referring to the fatal cattle disease Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy.

Dutch Farm Minister Jozias Van Aartsen will highlight the 1997/98 farm price package and the need to continue farm reforms started in 1992 when he presents the Dutch EU presidency's programme to farm ministers on January 20.

The Netherlands, an important dairy producer, also intends to start serious discussion on reform of the EU's milk quota scheme, though this would not be directly linked to beef reforms, Dutch officials said.
MAD COW CRISIS
BSE: British Farm Minister Douglas Hogg told EU farm ministers last month that he would present proposals early in 1997, probably February, to exempt certified herds from the world ban.
The ban was imposed by the EU last March after London disclosed that BSE could be transmitted to humans in the form of Creutzfeldt Jacob Disease.
Northern Irish herds certified free of the disease could be the first to be exempted, Dutch farm ministry spokesman Henri Kruithof told reporters in The Hague last week.
Northern Irish herds are generally fed on grass -- unlike English herds which were given contaminated meat and bone meal -- and their movements are tracked by a computerised system.
Kruithof cautioned against any early easing of the ban, saying it would take at least two years to extend the tracking system to the whole of Britain.
The British proposals would have to be agreed by the Commission, EU veterinary committees and member states.
Several countries, notably Germany, are expected to resist any early easing of the ban while uncertainties exist about the cause and eradication of the disease.
Exemption of certified herds would be the first step towards lifting the world ban on British beef exports under an agreement reached at the EU summit in Florence last June.
It followed Britain's announcement last month that it will cull an extra 100,000 cattle most at risk to BSE. The cull is the fifth and final pre-condition set under the Florence accord.
But the cull could be raised, depending on scientific advice due in March on data that BSE can be passed from cows to calves.

BEEF REFORMS: The Commission is due to present proposals by the end of April for long-term measures to cut production to bring it into line with a fall in demand caused by the public health scare over mad cow disease.
When farm ministers agreed a package of short-term measures last October, they asked the Commission to draft further proposals within six months so that a decision could be taken by the end of 1997.

Longer term measures could include a reduction in national quotas of male cattle whose producers receive EU subsidies, incentives for less intensive grass-fed herds and a restructuring of livestock production.
A reinforced beef promotion campaign and a reduction in carcass weight limits for cattle sold into intervention stores could also form part of the package.
On January 20, farm ministers are due to continue discussions on proposals to introduce cattle passport and beef labelling schemes intended to help restore consumer confidence.
PRICE PACKAGE
Commission price proposals for 1997/98 (July/June), expected early February, are again likely to be fairly modest, Commission officials said.

Farm support prices and compensation payments look set to remain unchanged although Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler may again try to cut monthly increases in grain storage payments. A fresh bid may be made to cut monthly sugar storage refunds.
"The package is likely to be very small...mainly a rollover of existing measures," said a Commission official said.
FARM REFORMS
1) OLIVE OIL: The Commission is expected to present proposals on January 23 to reform the olive oil marketing regime, simplifying subsidies and curbing costly fraud.
Southern European farmers are concerned that the reforms will lead to a reduction in both quality and income.
The reform will be the latest in a series started in 1992 with oilseeds and cereals, aimed at removing surplus production and cutting costs.
2) TOBACCO: On January 20 farm ministers are due to start discussing a Commission report urging reforms to improve tobacco quality and incentives for farmers to stop growing it.
The report was adopted on December 18 in spite of strong criticism that the continuation of tobacco subsidies hindered efforts to curb smoking-related deaths.
But Fischler argued successfully that ending the subsidies would put 300,000 people out of work in Greece and Italy with little prospect of finding other employment.

3) DAIRY REFORM: Although the current milk quota system expires at the end of March 2000, the Dutch are keen to press ahead with discussion of reforms to prepare for the next round of world farm trade negotiations starting in 1999 and the EU's enlargement eastwards.
The Commission is due to present a discussion paper, setting out options, in time for a preliminary discussion at an informal meeting of farm ministers in Domburg, Zeeland, from May 25-27.
